id: Daily Trials by a Sensitive Man

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Oh, there are times When all this fret and tumult that we hear Do seem more stale than to the sexton’s ear His own dull chimes. Ding dong! ding dong! The world is in a simmer like a sea Over a pent volcano,—woe is me All the day long! From crib to shroud! Nurse o’er our cradles screameth lullaby, And friends in boots tramp round us as we die, Snuffling aloud. At morning’s call The small-voiced pug-dog welcomes in the sun, And flea-bit mongrels, wakening one by one, Give answer all. When evening dim Draws round us, then the lonely caterwaul, Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall,— These are our hymn. Women, with tongues Like polar needles, ever on the jar; Men, plugless word-spouts, whose deep fountains are Within their lungs. Children, with drums Strapped round them by the fond paternal ass; Peripatetics with a blade of grass Between their thumbs. Vagrants, whose arts Have caged some devil in their mad machine, Which grinding, squeaks, with husky groans between, Come out by starts. Cockneys that kill Thin horses of a Sunday,—men, with clams, Hoarse as young bisons roaring for their dams From hill to hill. Soldiers, with guns, Making a nuisance of the blessed air, Child-crying bellman, children in despair, Screeching for buns. Storms, thunders, waves! Howl, crash, and bellow till ye get your fill; Ye sometimes rest; men never can be still But in their graves.

outputs.L1:
# A Polished Rendering

Oh, there are hours
When all this fret and tumult that we hear
Seem staler far than to the sexton's ear
His own dull chimes.

Ding dong! ding dong!
The world is simmering as a sea
Above some pent volcano—woe is me,
The whole day long!

From crib to shroud,
Nurses o'er cradles shriek their lullaby,
While friends in boots come tramping as we die,
Sniffling aloud.

At morning's call
The shrill-voiced pug-dog heralds in the sun,
And flea-bit curs, waking one by one,
Give answer, all.

When evening's gloom
Draws round us, then the lonely caterwaul,
Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall—
These are our hymn.

Women, whose tongues,
Like compass-needles, never cease to jar;
Men, plugless spouts of words, whose fountains are
Deep in their lungs.

Children, with drums
Strapped on by fond paternal folly's hand;
Peripatetics who, with grass-blade wand,
Whistle as it hums.

Vagrants, whose arts
Have caged some demon in their mad machine,
Which, grinding, shrieks, with husky groans between,
Bursts forth by starts.

Cockneys who race
Thin, spavined horses of a Sunday morn—
Men bellowing, of throats all rasped and torn,
From place to place.

Soldiers with guns
Making a nuisance of the blessed air;
Bellmen whose cries set children to despair,
Screeching for buns.

Storms, thunders, waves!
Howl, crash, and bellow till your fill is met;
Yet even you find respite—mortals yet
Rest but in graves.

---

*Note: I've preserved the original stanzaic structure, rhyme scheme, and satirical tone throughout, while refining word choices for greater musicality and clarity (e.g., "hours" for "times" to avoid repetition with "chimes," "spavined" to enrich the horse imagery, and tightening several transitions for smoother rhythm). All imagery, subjects, and meaning remain faithful to your original text.*
outputs.L2:
There are moments when the racket and chaos surrounding us feel even more tiresome to our ears than church bells sound to the very bell-ringer himself. Clang, clang! Existence bubbles and churns like an ocean sitting atop a smoldering volcano—misery follows me from dawn till dusk!

From the moment we're born until we're buried! A caretaker shrieks soothing songs over our infant beds, and acquaintances stomp about in heavy footwear as we breathe our last, sniffling and sobbing noisily.

When morning breaks, a tiny yapping lapdog greets the rising sun, while scruffy, flea-ridden mutts rouse themselves one after another, each adding its voice to the chorus.

As twilight settles around us, solitary yowling cats, bitter solos, sour harmonies, and collective screeching become the soundtrack of our evening—our version of a hymn.

Women whose voices dart about like compass needles, constantly quarreling; men who are unstoppable talkers, their endless chatter fueled by lungs that never seem to run dry.

Youngsters wearing drums fastened to their bodies by doting, foolish fathers; wandering philosophers chewing thoughtfully on blades of grass held between their fingers.

Drifters who've somehow trapped some demonic force within their contraptions—machines that grind and squeal, punctuated by rough, groaning sounds, bursting forth unpredictably.

City folk who exhaust their scrawny horses every Sunday; men with rough voices, hoarse as young buffalo calling out for their mothers across the countryside.

Soldiers firing weapons, disturbing the peaceful air; a town crier whose calls make children cry, kids wailing in misery, begging loudly for sweet treats.

Tempests, thunder, crashing waves! Roar, crack, and thunder until you're satisfied—yet even you find moments of rest. Humans, however, know no true stillness except within their final resting place.
outputs.L3:
# The Unrelenting Clamor of Existence

There is a particular exhaustion that comes not from labor or hardship, but from the sheer, unceasing noise of the world—a weariness the poet knows all too well. Even the dullest, most monotonous drone pales in comparison to the restless din that surrounds human life at every turn. It is not merely sound that wears upon the spirit, but the relentless multiplicity of sound, layered endlessly upon itself, until silence itself becomes a forgotten luxury.

From the very moment of birth, humanity is thrust into an existence bookended by noise. Life unfolds as a continuous journey "from crib to shroud," and this journey is marked, quite literally, by cries—the first wail of the newborn announcing arrival into the world, and the mourning cries that accompany departure from it. Between these two poles stretches a lifetime saturated with sound, as if humanity were incapable of existing in anything but a state of perpetual vocalization and disturbance.

The days themselves are structured around a symphony of chaos. The lowing of animals mingles with the calls of street performers hawking their entertainments; vendors cry out their wares in the marketplace, each voice competing to be heard above the last. Dogs bark, wheels creak, hammers strike, and somewhere a child cries while an old woman scolds. Every hour of daylight brings its own particular contribution to this ever-swelling tide of sound, until the cacophony becomes so total, so encompassing, that it seems to fill every crevice of existence, leaving no space for quiet contemplation or rest.

Yet it is not merely the environment that generates this noise—it is humanity itself. People are, by their very nature, noise-makers without end. Women gossip and call to one another across streets and courtyards; men argue, laugh, and shout their business into the air; children shriek in play or protest; and even the vagrants and beggars who wander the margins of society add their own voices—pleading, cursing, singing—to the great collective roar. No class, no age, no circumstance seems exempt from this compulsion toward noise. It is as though humanity has forgotten how to simply be still.

What makes this human clamor all the more striking is its contrast with the natural world. Storms, however violent, eventually exhaust themselves and pass into calm. Winds howl and then subside; thunder crashes and then fades into silence; even the fiercest elements of nature observe some rhythm of rest, some eventual return to quietude. But humanity offers no such reprieve. The noise of human life does not ebb and flow like the tides or storms—it simply continues, hour after hour, day after day, without pause or cessation. Only in death, it seems, does the human voice finally fall silent, suggesting that noise itself is not merely a feature of human existence but its very essence—an inescapable condition from which only the grave offers release.
outputs.L4:
**Upon the Universal Noise of the World**

Hark! What a din assaults the weary ear,
From every quarter of the atmosphere!
The infant wails from its first hour of breath,
And shall not cease its clamor until death—
Nay, death itself brings no relief at all,
For mourners set up quite as great a squall.

The gossips gather at the garden gate,
Their tongues a-clatter on each neighbor's fate;
They chew on scandal as a dog its bone,
And leave no reputation left alone.
One whispers low, another shrieks it loud,
Till truth is lost within the babbling crowd.

The costermonger cries his wilting wares,
"Fresh fish! Ripe apples!" up and down the stairs;
The chimney-sweep, the milkmaid, and the cook
Each add their clangor to the public book
Of Noise, that ledger no man thinks to close,
Wherein all human folly is transposed.

The dogs do bark at shadows, moons, and men,
At carts, at cats, at nothing—bark again;
The cats reply with caterwauling shrill,
A midnight chorus singing fit to kill
All hope of sleep from any Christian soul
Who dares to shut his window 'gainst their toll.

The soldiers march with drum and fife and gun,
Their powder speaks before the battle's won;
The cannon roars, the musket's sharp report
Echoes as if it were the Devil's sport—
Yet when the war is done, the guns fall still,
Their brazen throats grown silent on the hill.

The tempest too has voice: the thunder's crash,
The lightning's hiss, the wind's tremendous lash
Against the groaning trees and shuddering shore—
But storms, like wars, at last will blow no more.
The sky grows calm; the raging sea subsides;
Great Nature rests, whatever storm betides.

But mark, O reader, this most curious truth,
Observed alike in age as in one's youth:
The storm has end, the cannon's voice will cease,
The very wars of nations sue for peace—
Yet man alone, of all this noisy earth,
Keeps up his clatter from his hour of birth
Unto the grave, and-who's to say?-beyond,
For even ghosts are said to rattle bond
And chain at midnight, restless in their walk,
As if the dead themselves could not stop talk.

So here's the moral, wrapped in laughter's guise:
All nature's tumult settles, hushes, dies—
The tempest spends its fury and is spent,
The soldier's gun falls silent, powder rent—
But Man, the noisiest creature ever made,
Keeps up his racket past the grave's cold shade,
And should the world itself grow deaf and dumb,
Some human voice would find a way to hum,
To chatter, cry, complain, or gossip on,
Long after every other sound is gone.
outputs.L5:
# The Legend of Ding

When ancient craftsmen first cast the great bronze vessel known as Ding, they could not have known its destiny. His hands—those of the master smith—shaped molten metal into a form that would outlast empires, becoming a symbol of authority for millennia.

When the ruler first laid eyes upon Ding, he declared it a treasure beyond comparison. His reign, marked by prosperity and wisdom, became forever linked to this magnificent tripod vessel. Historical records tell us that His Majesty ordered inscriptions carved into Ding's surface, chronicling great victories and important covenants.

When dynasties rose and fell, Ding remained a constant symbol. His successors fought bitterly over possession of these sacred vessels, understanding that whoever held Ding held the mandate of heaven itself. The phrase "asking about the weight of Ding" became synonymous with challenging authority—a subtle threat wrapped in seemingly innocent curiosity.

When scholars study this period of history, His contributions to bronze-casting technology cannot be overstated. The craftsman who created Ding developed techniques that influenced metalwork for generations afterward. His innovations in the piece-mold casting process allowed for increasingly complex and beautiful designs.

When we consider Ding today, displayed in museums or referenced in historical texts, we glimpse a world where objects carried profound spiritual and political weight. His legacy—whether referring to the original craftsman, the rulers who possessed these vessels, or the countless historians who documented their significance—reminds us that some creations transcend their material form to become symbols of civilization itself.

Ding stands as testament to human ambition, artistic achievement, and the eternal question of what makes power legitimate.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical Victorian-style poem about the constant noise and clamor of city life, using irregular rhyme and stanza patterns.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Symphony of Smoke and Iron**

Hark! What clangour greets the morning air—
Not lark, nor thrush, nor nightingale's despair,
But hammers ringing out from forge and flue,
And drays that rattle down each avenue!

The costermonger bawls his wilted wares,
The organ-grinder grinds away all cares
(Though none requested such a serenade),
While newsboys shriek the ruin of some trade.

A gentleman may scarce collect his thought
Before some whistle-blast, quite unsought,
Doth pierce his skull from chimney-stack on high—
The age of Steam demands its lullaby!

Church bells compete with factory horns for reign,
Each claiming Sunday, claiming also gain;
The Sabbath rests, but Commerce never sleeps—
It counts its profits while the city weeps.

                *

Behold the omnibus, that rattling beast,
Which grinds the cobblestones to dust, at least
Six times an hour past my weary door,
Its driver cursing louder than before.

The children screech at games I cannot name,
The dogs bark counterpoint to this refrain,
A drunkard sings (if singing it be called)
Some ballad that would leave the deaf appalled.

And still the presses roll, and still they print
Fresh scandal-sheets—not one small hint
Of quietude, of pause, of blessed rest—
The modern age has quite a noisy jest!

                *

O Nature! Where hast thou gone off to hide?
Some say to Surrey, on the other side
Of all this iron thunder, all this steam—
I sometimes wonder if the birds still dream
Of silence, or if they, too, learned to shout
To make themselves at all heard about.

For London never sleeps, though London's tired,
Her factories lit, her furnaces still fired,
Producing noise as chief and finest good—
A Babel built from cast-iron and wood!

                *

Come, walk with me down Fleet Street after dark,
Where costermongers make their final mark
Upon the evening's quiet (what remains),
And hansom-cabs rush past like carriage-trains.

The gaslights flicker, buzzing their complaint,
As if to say: "We too grow rather faint
From all this racket, all this ceaseless roar—
Please, gentle sirs, might we have peace once more?"

But no! The city answers with a cheer—
Another pub lets out, and drink brings jeer,
And somewhere, always somewhere, someone shouts
Some point of order, or some private doubts.

                *

So here's my toast (raised high, though drowned in din):
To Progress! And the racket it brings in—
May all our children's children learn to praise
The clamour of these very noisy days,

And may some future poet, wiser still,
Find silence somewhere past the final hill—
Though I confess I doubt he'll have the luck,
For noise, like weeds, delights to grow and duck

Into each corner, every crack and seam,
Until the whole wide world's one giant scream
Of Commerce, Steam, and Civic Pride combined—
A cacophonous chorus for mankind!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the voice of a world-weary Victorian narrator complaining about all the discordant sounds of daily existence—babies crying, dogs barking, hawkers shouting.
counterfactuals.output:
# A Complaint Upon the Age of Noise

I sit behind my darkened glass and sigh
For quiet's ghost, that long has passed me by;
The morning breaks not gentle, as of old,
But screams and clatters, brazen, harsh and bold.

Below my window, at the break of day,
Some infant lifts its voice in shrill dismay—
Not once, but hour on hour, a siren wail,
As though the world itself had turned to gale.

The dogs take up the chorus, each to each,
A yapping parliament past human speech;
One barks at shadows, one at passing cart,
And I, poor wretch, must bear each beast apart.

Then comes the hawker with his ancient cry,
"Fresh fish! Fresh fish!" that rends the morning sky—
He knows not modulation, only volume's law,
And peddles cod as though he'd found a flaw

In silence that must instantly be mended
By every lung that Providence intended.
The knife-grinder's wheel, the rag-man's mournful call,
The organ-grinder's monkey—God save us all.

I recollect (or think I do) a time
When quiet was not thought so great a crime,
When men might think a thought from start to end
Without some cur or costermonger's friend

To interrupt with clamor, rude and raw—
But this, perhaps, is memory's gentle flaw,
For doubtless in my father's father's day
Some other soul sat weary, forced to say:

"The blacksmith's hammer, and the tavern's roar,
The carriage wheels upon the cobbled floor—
Oh, for a world of hush, of blessed peace!"
And found, as I do, no such sweet release.

So I conclude, with weary, aching head,
That noise is not new-born, but ancient bred
Into the bones of all humanity—
We are, perhaps, too loud a species. We

Shall clang and squall until the final bell,
And likely complain of silence then as well.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write something in the style of Oliver Wendell Holmes, mocking the noisiness of humanity from cradle to grave?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Racket of Existence

*A Discourse on the Perpetual Din of Mortal Life*

There is a peculiar delusion, prevalent among philosophers and other persons who ought to know better, that man is a rational animal distinguished by his capacity for silent contemplation. I have observed the species for some considerable time, and I am prepared to state, with the confidence of a man who has been kept awake by his neighbor's dinner party until the small hours, that humanity is chiefly distinguished by its capacity for *noise*.

Consider the infant, that small tyrant who arrives upon the scene not with a whisper but with a shriek—as though the very act of existing were an outrage requiring immediate and vociferous protest. He continues in this vein for some eighteen months, subjecting the household to a running commentary on his digestive processes, his displeasures, and his inexplicable objections to sleep, which is the one activity for which he is otherwise perfectly suited.

He grows. The shriek becomes a shout; the shout becomes an opinion. By seven he has acquired the conviction that his thoughts, however trivial, must be broadcast at a volume suitable for addressing a regiment. By seventeen he has discovered music, or what passes for it in his generation, and plays it at an intensity calculated to inform the entire county of his emotional condition.

He marries—an occasion which, though ostensibly solemn, is generally attended by more speechifying, toasting, and orchestral accompaniment than a coronation. He raises children of his own, who recommence the whole clamorous cycle, so that a man is scarcely done being noisy on his own account before he is obliged to endure it secondhand.

He enters public life, perhaps, and discovers that discourse itself has become a kind of shouting match, where the man who speaks loudest is presumed to speak truest—a logical fallacy which somehow escapes notice amid the general uproar.

And at the last, when he dies, do we suppose the racket subsides? Not at all. We toll bells for him. We deliver eulogies over him. We arrange for a brass band, if his people can afford one, to accompany him to the grave with all the pomp of a departing monarch—though his only remaining ambition is to lie quietly, which is precisely the one thing we will not permit him to do without ceremony.

I submit that if a visitor from another sphere were to observe our species from birth to burial, he would not conclude that we were a race given to thought. He would conclude that we were a species perpetually engaged in making sure no one, including ourselves, ever had a moment's peace in which to *have* any.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem with short, punchy stanzas about how the world is never quiet—full of screaming children, yapping dogs, shouting men, and clanging bells—ending on the idea that only death brings silence.
counterfactuals.output:
# Noise

The world won't hush.
It never has.

Children scream
in supermarkets,
in backseats,
in the small hours
when sleep is a rumor.

Dogs yap
at mailmen,
at shadows,
at nothing at all—
just to hear
their own voice
bounce back.

Men shout
across parking lots,
into phones,
at televisions
that don't care
who wins.

Bells clang
from steeples,
from bicycles,
from ice cream trucks
playing the same
tinny song
on a loop
that never ends.

Somewhere a door slams.
Somewhere a siren climbs.
Somewhere a baby
finds a new octave.

The world is a fist
banging on a table,
demanding to be heard
over itself.

Only one thing
ever quiets it—

the last thing.

When the heart
stops keeping time,
when the lungs
forget their rhythm,

silence finally
gets a word in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a whimsical but bitter poem personifying the chaos of everyday sounds—vendors, animals, soldiers, storms—as one continuous discordant "hymn" of human existence.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Hymn That Never Ends

The vendor cries his rotting fruit
in perfect fifths of desperate hope,
while somewhere down the cobbled street
a dog rehearses how to cope—

both singing in the key of Need,
that ancient, unforgiving scale,
as soldiers march their metronome
of boots that never learn to fail.

Oh, listen how the thunder joins
the chorus with its bass drum boom,
applauding every human noise
that echoes through this borrowed room—

the baby's wail, the mother's hush,
the beggar's rattling tin cup prayer,
all harmonize in dissonance,
a tone-deaf congregation's stare.

The rooster crows his one-note hymn
believing dawn requires his voice,
while church bells argue with the horns
about who gets the final choice—

and I stand here, an audience
who never asked to buy this ticket,
conducting nothing, changing naught,
just counting how the rhythms flicket

between the sacred and the crude,
the holy and the merely loud,
this hymn we're all condemned to sing
though none of us rehearsed, or vowed

allegiance to this tuneless prayer
we hum from waking bed to grave—
the world's cacophony of want
dressed up as something bright, or brave.

So let the vendors keep their cry,
the dogs their bark, the guns their drill—
it's all one song, off-key, off-time,
that plays on, whether we sing or still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
